title: A contact path for an independent hotel
metaTitle: Contact path for an independent hotel
excerpt: The contact page should say who replies, how soon, and what to have ready. Checking dates stays the main action. Ten fields will lose the guest.
alt: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp.
caption: Someone is actually at the desk. A contact page should say who that is. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a guest use the contact form?
faqs.answer: When the date checker cannot hold the question: a late train, a dog, a mobility issue, or a buyout of the house. Ordinary nights should go through check dates. Say that at the top of the contact page so the inbox is not a second booking engine.

faqs.question: What should the form ask for?
faqs.answer: A name, an email, the dates, the room, and the question. Party size matters when it changes the room. Drop company, job title, budget, and how they heard of you. Tell guests not to paste a card number into the box.

faqs.question: What should the confirmation say?
faqs.answer: Who reads the message, by when, and what it does not do, such as holding a room. Use a window you have kept on recent mail, including weekends if you are slow then. Match that text in the email receipt, because the guest will keep the email and lose the page.

markdown:
An independent hotel contact page should tell a traveler comparing three stays what happens after they reach out, how soon a person replies, and what to have ready. The action of the site is still to check dates. A form with ten fields is a way to lose the people who had a simple question and a phone in their hand.

WCAG's understandable principle is the right standard for this page. The form should explain itself: labels on the fields, errors that say what to fix, and a result the guest can interpret. A form that only a staff member understands is a locked door with a nicer typeface.

## Dates first, messages second

Most people do not need to contact you. They need a night that is free, at the rate you published, in the room you photographed. The contact page should say that, at the top, with a link that checks dates. Treat the form as the path for everything the checker cannot hold.

Say which questions belong here. A train that arrives after the door is locked. A mobility need the stair count does not fully answer. A dog. A request to book every room. A correction to a reservation that already exists. If you list these, guests self-sort. If you do not, they will use the form for ordinary nights, and you will answer booking mail by hand until you resent the website.

Put the date link above the form, in the same words as the header. "Check dates" should not become "Inquire" on this page only. One verb for the main action. The form is the side door, labeled as a side door, without shame. Side doors are how small houses handle exceptions well.

If you are often full, say what the checker shows, and do not invite people to "just email" for nights the system already closed. Exceptions you cannot honor become a second, shadow inventory. That inventory is how double bookings and tired replies start.

## What happens after they send it

The confirmation on the screen has to be specific. "Sent" is not enough. Say who receives it, in a role the guest can picture: the person at the desk, not "the team," not a ticket number with no human. Say whether they should expect a reply in the same place, by email, and whether a phone call is something you do or something you do not do.

If you do not work overnight, say so in the confirmation as well as beside the form. A message sent at 1 a.m. should not sound as if someone is awake and composing a welcome. Promise the next window you actually keep. If that window is "by the end of the next morning," write that, and mean it. A faster promise you miss is worse than a slower promise you keep.

Say what you will not do. You will not hold a room without the checker or a card, if that is the rule. You will not redesign a rate by email. You will not promise a quiet lane you have already described as busy. Limits in the confirmation prevent a hopeful reading of a vague thank-you.

Copy the same sentences into the email receipt, if you send one. The guest will lose the page and keep the email. Those two texts are one conversation. Write them together.

## How fast, said in a way you can keep

Speed is a fact about your rota, not a brand attribute. Look at the last twenty messages and write the window that would have been true for all of them, not the window that was true on your best Tuesday. Publish that. Then staff it. A page that says "we reply within the hour" while the only person who sees the inbox is at breakfast service is a fiction.

If the window differs by day, say the days. "Weekday mornings, before noon. Weekends, in the evening after arrivals." Independent hotels often have this shape and hide it because it looks less polished than a 24-hour call center. The guest is not comparing you to a call center. They are comparing you to two other small houses. The one that states a true window feels safer.

Name a backup. When the person who reads the inbox is away, who reads it, and does the window change? If the answer is "nobody, and we should have said," change the page before the holiday, not after the angry thread. The about page's names should match this duty. If Luis reads the form, Luis can be mentioned here without a biography.

Do not display a live chat button you do not attend. A chat that sleeps is a form with worse expectations. If you can truly answer in the moment for certain hours, say the hours and close the widget outside them. An always-on badge that is not always on trains guests to think the house is careless.

## What to have ready

Tell them what makes a reply possible. Dates, even if approximate. The room they mean, using your real room names. The question in one or two sentences. A phone number only if you might need to call, and not as a toll for a simple note. For a dog: the size, and whether it will be alone in the room. For a late arrival: the hour. For a buyout: how many rooms, and whether they need dinner you may not serve.

Ask for an email you can reply to, and a name. That is the core. Party size matters when it changes the room. It does not matter for a question about the stair. Required fields should be the ones you need for this message, not the ones a marketing tool likes to store.

Tell them not to include a card number. If payment happens, it happens in the booking system, not in a contact box. Say that beside the form so a helpful guest does not paste sensitive numbers into an inbox that was never meant to hold them.

If a question needs a document, such as a company invoice detail, say which question that is. Do not ask every guest for a postal address. Most of them are trying to book a room, not receive a letter.

## The ten-field form

Count the fields. Name, email, dates, the room, and the question will cover almost every legitimate message. A fifth field for party size is reasonable. A form becomes hostile as it approaches ten: company, job title, country, a budget range, "how did you hear about us," a newsletter checkbox that is already on, a category dropdown that repeats the question, a postal address, a required phone, a second phone, a captcha that fails on the mobile network they are using.

Each extra field is a reason to go back to the other tab and book the hotel that let them check dates. The comparison is not theoretical. It is open on the phone while they decide whether your form is worth it.

"How did you hear about us" is your marketing question. Ask it later, if you must, of people who already stayed. Do not charge the pre-stay question with it. Budget ranges are similarly yours. The rate page should have made the shape clear enough that a budget interrogation is unnecessary. If it did not, fix the rate page. Do not interrogate the guest for the repair.

Use labels that stay visible, not placeholders that vanish when typing starts. WCAG's demand that the form be understandable shows up here in a small way: a guest should be able to check what they are filling after they have started to fill it. Errors should name the field. "Invalid input" is not an error message. "Add an email so we can reply" is.

The submit button should say "Send to the desk" or "Send the question," not "Submit." After it is pressed, leave it in a state that does not invite a double send. Show the confirmation in the same page, where the form was, so a phone user does not have to hunt for a banner.

## Questions the checker cannot answer

Write three short examples near the form, so the box is less frightening. "We land at 11:30 p.m. Is the door still answered?" "Is the courtyard room possible with a small dog?" "Can we take all four rooms on 12 May?" Examples teach scope. They also teach tone. A guest will mimic the length you show them. If your examples are two lines, your replies will be easier to write than if the form looks like a visa application.

Answer the common three on the page itself, above the form, if the answer is stable. A stair count does not need a correspondence. A dog rule does not need a correspondence. Every answer you can publish is a message you will not receive. The form gets sharper as the site gets more specific. That is the relationship between this page and the rest of the site.

For questions you cannot answer in public, the form is right. Medical equipment, a sensitive celebration, a complaint about a past stay. Say that a person reads these, and say the window again.

Link to the proof and the rate when the question is usually a worry you have already handled. "If you are asking about the lane, the small-double page shows it at 4 p.m." You are allowed to point at your own honesty. It reduces mail, and it respects the guest who is willing to read.

## Where the path sits

Link the contact path from the footer and from any page whose content creates exceptions: dogs, arrival hours, the whole house. Do not link it as the main button on the homepage. The main button checks dates. A site with two equal buttons, "Book" and "Contact," will receive booking requests in the inbox and then complain about the guests. The guests followed the path you weighted equally.

The page's own heading should say that this is a question, not a booking. "Ask the desk" is clear. "Get in touch" is a fog. "Contact us" is acceptable if the first sentence repairs it. Prefer the clearer heading. The traveler is skimming, and the heading is the skim.

Make sure the address, the entrance note, and a phone number for arrival day are on this page even if they are also elsewhere. People open "contact" to find the door. A form without a door is a strange omission, and it generates messages that only ask where you are. Publish the door. Then the form can be about the harder things.

When the path is this tight, the remaining risk is everything you still publish that confuses the same traveler. [What to take off the site so the room and the dates can do their work](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-an-independent-hotel) is the next piece. It is the edit that protects the contact page from becoming a dumping ground.

To see sites that keep a single, obvious next step, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The contact page should feel as plain as a good front desk: dates first, a person second, and no paperwork that the stay did not require.
